newsitem.title: UK: SPORT-BRITISH ATHLETES GET LOTTERY HANDOUT.
newsitem.headline: SPORT-BRITISH ATHLETES GET LOTTERY HANDOUT.

text.p: Britain took a major step towards improving their meagre medal haul from this summer's Olympics on Thursday by announcing a 40 million pounds ($64 million) handout of National Lottery money to sportsmen and women.

Half of the cash will go to individual competitors for training and competition, the rest will provide more full-time coaches, help identify new talent and enable Britain to stage major championships.
It is the biggest-ever funding package for sport in Britain and comes in the wake of the country's disapppointing collection of one gold, eight silver and six bronze medals in Atlanta.
The programme follows relaxation of the Lottery rules which previously restricted handouts to "bricks and mortar" projects like leisure centres and swimming pools.
The handout was announced by the Sports Council whose chairman, Sir Rodney Walker, estimated that in the first year alone around 4,500 competitors would benefit.

"Many people criticised us heavily for appearing to drag our feet after the Atlanta Olympics with a loud clamour for funds as the solution to the problems many encountered before and at the Games," he said.
"The truth is we could have launched his programme earlier but we weren't ready.
He said the delay resulted from a period of consultation "with those who mattered.
"As a result of this careful planning the programme is bigger, better and directly meets needs of the competitors and coaches."

Sir Rodney added: "It is not a quick fix but a long-term plan. It will mean that those individuals who dedicate their lives to bringing medals back to this country will not pay a financial price as so many have done in the past."
He hoped the results would be seen at the Sydney Olympics in 2000 and the Commonwealth Games in Manchester in 2002."
Top cyclist Chris Boardman said: "This will stop talent from giving up and enable them to commit themselves to a life of sport."
Other athletes echoed Boardman's feelings. The 400 metres silver medallist, Roger Black, said: "It is notpeople like me and Linford Christie who need the money.
"It is the young people who will be lost to sport because they do not have the financing who need it most."
